title: ExxonMobil (NYSE:XOM) Stock Jumps 1.2% - Still a Buy? - MarketBeat

ExxonMobil Corporation (NYSE:XOM - Get Free Report) shot up 1.2% on Tuesday. The company traded as high as $174.89 and last traded at $174.25. 11,376,525 shares were traded during trading, a decline of 37% from the average daily volume of 18,041,188 shares. The stock had previously closed at $172.15. Here are the key news stories impacting ExxonMobil this week: A number of equities analysts have recently issued reports on XOM shares. JPMorgan Chase & Co. upped their price objective on ExxonMobil from $158.00 to $166.00 and gave the stock an "overweight" rating in a report on Monday, August 3rd. Morgan Stanley raised their price objective on ExxonMobil from $168.00 to $177.00 and gave the company an "overweight" rating in a report on Wednesday, August 19th. Barclays dropped their target price on ExxonMobil from $182.00 to $177.00 and set an "overweight" rating for the company in a research report on Monday, August 17th. BNP Paribas Exane cut their target price on ExxonMobil from $165.00 to $155.00 and set a "neutral" rating for the company in a research note on Friday, July 17th. Finally, The Goldman Sachs Group increased their price target on shares of ExxonMobil from $168.00 to $169.00 and gave the company a "neutral" rating in a research report on Tuesday, September 22nd. Eleven equities research analysts have rated the stock with a Buy rating and fourteen have assigned a Hold rating to the company. Based on data from MarketBeat.com, ExxonMobil presently has an average rating of "Hold" and a consensus target price of $164.78. The company has a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.12, a quick ratio of 0.85 and a current ratio of 1.13. The firm has a 50-day moving average of $162.00 and a 200-day moving average of $154.23. The firm has a market capitalization of $722.26 billion, a P/E ratio of 22.43, a price-to-earnings-growth ratio of 0.99 and a beta of 0.21. ExxonMobil (NYSE:XOM - Get Free Report) last issued its earnings results on Friday, July 31st. The oil and gas company reported $3.52 earnings per share (EPS) for the quarter, missing the consensus estimate of $3.56 by ($0.04). ExxonMobil had a return on equity of 13.14% and a net margin of 8.88%. The firm had revenue of $114.53 billion during the quarter, compared to the consensus estimate of $109.94 billion. During the same quarter in the prior year, the business posted $1.64 EPS.  On average, equities research analysts anticipate that ExxonMobil Corporation will post 12.40 EPS for the current fiscal year. The business also recently disclosed a quarterly dividend, which was paid on Thursday, September 10th. Shareholders of record on Monday, August 17th were issued a $1.03 dividend. The ex-dividend date was Monday, August 17th. This represents a $4.12 annualized dividend and a yield of 2.4%. ExxonMobil's dividend payout ratio is 53.02%. Several large investors have recently bought and sold shares of XOM. GQG Partners LLC lifted its stake in shares of ExxonMobil by 153.3% during the second quarter. GQG Partners LLC now owns 16,877,523 shares of the oil and gas company's stock worth $2,307,497,000 after buying an additional 10,214,420 shares during the period.  Quantum Portfolio Management LLC acquired a new position in shares of ExxonMobil in the 1st quarter valued at $965,932,000.  Arrowstreet Capital Limited Partnership purchased a new position in ExxonMobil in the 1st quarter worth $766,345,000.  Diamant Asset Management Inc. raised its stake in ExxonMobil by 17,312.4% in the 1st quarter. Diamant Asset Management Inc. now owns 2,183,864 shares of the oil and gas company's stock worth $370,514,000 after acquiring an additional 2,171,322 shares during the last quarter.  Finally, Employees Provident Fund Board acquired a new stake in ExxonMobil during the 4th quarter worth about $238,970,000. 61.80% of the stock is owned by institutional investors. The integrated major sits at the center of the sector as one of the most closely watched barometers of how the group responds when oil prices strengthen rather than soften. The tone across energy equities brightened as crude firmed from earlier lows, with the commodity backdrop acting as the dominant driver for the oil and gas group. Because the company earns across the full chain, from the wellhead to the fuel pump, it tends to reflect shifts in the barrel quickly, and the steadier reading on prices set a constructive mood for the wider complex. Crude prices anchor the earnings engine of every large producer, so even modest moves in the barrel ripple through revenue, cash generation and spending plans. When oil firms, upstream barrels fetch stronger realizations, and the improved pricing tends to flow through the reported results of the integrated majors. The recent firming came as exporters signaled a restrained approach to adding barrels, easing concern about an oversupplied market. Steadier prices support the economics of drilling programs and give operators more confidence to maintain measured capital spending across their asset base. The company is an integrated energy major, meaning it operates across exploration and production, refining, marketing and chemicals. That structure gives it a diversified earnings base, so weakness in one segment can be cushioned by strength in another, a quality that tends to smooth results through commodity cycles. Upstream, the firm develops oil and natural gas resources around the world. Downstream, it refines crude into fuels and lubricants and markets them through a global network. Its chemicals arm converts hydrocarbons into plastics and specialty materials used across many end markets, adding another layer to the earnings mix. The company operates a large upstream portfolio spanning onshore and offshore assets. Its position in the Permian Basin of West Texas and New Mexico has become a cornerstone of domestic output, prized for low operating costs and quick cycle times that let crews adjust activity as the market shifts. Beyond the Permian, the firm develops major offshore projects, including notable deepwater output off the coast of Guyana and liquefied natural gas ventures spread across several regions. This geographic spread lets the producer balance short-cycle shale barrels against longer-lived conventional projects. On the refining side, the company runs a global system of plants that turn crude into gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and other products. Refining margins hinge on the gap between crude costs and finished-fuel prices, a spread that can widen or narrow independently of the barrel itself and often moves counter to upstream swings. The chemicals business supplies building-block materials to packaging, automotive and construction customers. Demand there tracks broad industrial activity, giving the segment a different rhythm from the fuels market and reinforcing the diversified nature of the overall enterprise. Large energy producers have leaned on measured spending in recent years, directing cash toward their most efficient barrels while keeping balance sheets sturdy. That approach aims to keep operations resilient whether crude firms or fades, a discipline the market has rewarded with steadier sentiment. The company has emphasized cost reduction and structural efficiency across its assets, targeting lower break-even levels so projects stay workable even when prices ease. Such discipline is a recurring theme across the group as operators prioritize durable cash generation over rapid volume growth. Across the wider set of US Oil and Gas Stocks, a firmer barrel tends to lift the whole complex at once, from the largest integrated majors to smaller shale-focused operators and the oilfield service firms that supply them. The group frequently trades as a block when the commodity sets the tone. Sentiment toward the sector has swung with the crude market through the year, and the recent steadying helped the group find firmer ground. As one of the most widely tracked names in the space, the integrated major often acts as a reference point for how the broad energy trade is leaning. Natural gas has grown into a larger part of the story for the big producers as global demand for cleaner-burning fuel expands. Liquefied natural gas, chilled for shipment across oceans, links domestic supply to customers in Europe and Asia and has become a meaningful pillar of the long-term asset base. The company participates in LNG ventures spread across several continents, giving it exposure to a market that many expect to keep expanding as nations seek reliable fuel. Gas pricing can move on its own cadence, adding another variable alongside the crude market. The firming in crude arrived as third-quarter reporting season got underway across corporate America, with large banks and other heavyweights stepping forward in mid-October. Energy producers report their quarterly results against the commodity prices that prevailed through the period, so the direction of oil in the quarter frames expectations. Market participants watch quarterly updates from the majors for color on production volumes, spending plans and cash generation. The reporting window tends to concentrate attention on the sector and can amplify day-to-day moves when crude is already active. The large producers face a long-run shift as economies work toward lower-carbon energy. The company has directed capital toward lower-emission ventures such as carbon capture and storage, hydrogen and lithium development, aiming to build businesses that fit a changing energy landscape. These lower-carbon efforts sit alongside the core oil and gas operations rather than replacing them, reflecting a view that conventional fuels will remain central for many years even as newer lines take shape. How quickly those ventures scale remains a key theme for the sector. Energy equities rarely move in isolation. Global growth trends, currency swings, interest-rate expectations and geopolitics all feed into the crude market and, in turn, into the producers. A steadier barrel often coincides with easing concern about demand or supply disruptions. The latest firming leaned on signals that major exporters would add barrels only gradually, together with resilient consumption. Those crosscurrents can reverse quickly, which is why the sector tends to track the commodity tape closely from one session to the next. As one of the largest members of the S&P 500, the integrated major carries significant weight within the energy portion of the broad benchmark. Moves in the stock can nudge sector gauges and often serve as shorthand for how the energy trade is faring on a given day. Its sheer scale, global asset base and long operating history keep it among the most scrutinized names in the market. That visibility means commentary about crude frequently circles back to the company as a reference for the wider group. The producer has emphasized efficient barrels, cost control and reliable project execution as central operating priorities. Advancing low-cost developments in the Permian and offshore Guyana while sustaining downstream and chemicals output remains the core of the day-to-day focus. Keeping operations dependable through commodity swings is a recurring aim across the majors, and the company has framed steady execution as the way to navigate a market that can turn without warning. The firmer crude backdrop offers a more supportive setting for that work. The integrated major carries one of the longest dividend records in the broad market, having paid and steadily raised its quarterly cash distribution over many decades. That track record keeps the stock prominent among energy names that distribute cash to the owners of the shares, and the payout tends to draw attention whenever crude moves. Steady cash generation across the chain underpins the distribution even when the barrel softens, a quality that the market watches as a gauge of financial health. The firmer crude backdrop tends to ease any concern about the sustainability of such payouts across the group of large producers. Underpinning the business is a deep base of proved reserves spread across continents, from shale acreage in the Permian to deepwater barrels offshore and gas resources tied to export ventures. Reserve depth measures how long a producer can sustain output before new discoveries are needed. Replacing produced barrels through fresh development and exploration remains a central task, since reserves deplete as wells age. The company devotes meaningful effort to adding resources that keep the production base durable over the long run. Downstream earnings hinge on the crack spread, the gap between the cost of crude and the prices fetched by refined fuels. That spread can widen when fuel demand runs ahead of refining capacity and narrow when plants run flat out, moving on a cadence distinct from the barrel itself. Because the company refines at scale, swings in the crack spread feed directly into its downstream results. When upstream pricing softens, a healthy refining margin can cushion the blow, illustrating the balance that the integrated model is built to provide. The enterprise employs tens of thousands of people across exploration, refining, chemicals and corporate functions, operating in many countries and across several continents. That scale demands complex logistics to move crude, fuels and materials around the world. Managing such a sprawling operation calls for deep technical expertise and disciplined project execution. The breadth of the workforce and asset base is part of what keeps the company among the most closely followed names in global energy. Advances in drilling and completion technology have reshaped the economics of shale, letting operators extract more from each well while trimming the cost per barrel. The company has leaned on such techniques to drive down break-even levels across its core acreage. Longer lateral wells, refined fracturing designs and data-driven planning help crews lift more crude from the same footprint. Efficiency gains of this kind have been a defining theme across the shale era and continue to shape how the majors allocate activity. Crude is a global commodity, so events far from any single field can move prices. Supply disruptions, sanctions, conflict near major shipping lanes and decisions by large exporters all feed into the barrel and, in turn, into the producers that depend on it. The recent firming owed much to signals that major exporters would add supply only gradually, keeping the market from tipping into glut. A diversified global footprint helps the company weather regional shocks that might strike a single-basin operator harder. Global consumption of oil and gas shapes the backdrop for every producer. Demand from transport, aviation, shipping, petrochemicals and power generation drives the call on crude, and shifts in economic growth across major regions feed directly into how much the world consumes. Emerging economies have accounted for a growing share of demand growth, while mature markets lean toward efficiency and electrification. The balance between these forces helps set the tone for the barrel, and steadier demand readings tend to accompany the firmer crude that lifted the integrated major alongside the wider group. Energy is a capital-intensive business, and the pace of spending across the industry shapes supply years down the line. When producers trim budgets, fewer barrels reach the market later; when they spend freely, supply can build and weigh on prices. The measured spending of recent years has kept the pipeline of new barrels restrained. That restraint has been a defining feature of the current cycle, as operators favor efficient development over aggressive expansion. A firmer barrel can tempt the industry to lift activity, though the discipline shown so far has kept the supply response gradual rather than abrupt. Energy equities are prone to sharp swings because they ride a commodity that can move quickly on supply news, demand signals and geopolitics. Day-to-day moves in the stock often mirror the crude tape, and the group can gyrate even when the broad market is calm. Understanding that the sector trades with the barrel helps frame the recent firming: as oil steadied, energy names found support, and the most widely tracked producers tended to lead the move. Such swings cut both ways, which is why the commodity remains the central thread running through the whole group. For the broad US market, energy serves as a bellwether for inflation pressures and industrial health, since fuel costs feed into nearly every corner of the economy. A firmer barrel can lift the energy group even on days when technology or other sectors drag on the headline indexes. That dynamic was on display as oil steadied while parts of the market stayed choppy, leaving energy names among the firmer corners of the tape. The integrated major, given its size and reach, remains a focal point whenever the crude conversation heats up. title: Guyana's government reconsidering LNG project after Exxon Mobil (XOM) told Guyana it will need more gas for reinjection, according to reports, citing sources - Newsquawk

Saudi Civil Defence says danger has passed in the Eastern Province Guyana's government reconsidering LNG project after Exxon Mobil (XOM) told Guyana it will need more gas for reinjection, according to reports, citing sources Fed's Williams (voter) sees no need for rate hike in 2027 at this time; still believe disinflationary forces are at play On the Newsquawk feed at 18:14, 20 minutes before this page. The tension here is a standard one in frontier offshore developments: associated gas that a government wants monetised through LNG or domestic power competes with the operator's need to reinject gas for reservoir pressure maintenance and crude recovery. Reinjection demands of this kind have historically risen as fields mature and production profiles are better understood, and in past episodes of this kind the operator's reservoir case has tended to prevail on technical grounds, with governments re-scoping or delaying gas monetisation plans rather than overriding the operator. The actors matter: Exxon's position in Guyana is built on a production-sharing framework that has been contentious domestically, so the government's 'reconsideration' reads as a negotiation posture as much as an engineering verdict, and disputes over gas disposition have been a recurring friction point between the two. What is worth watching is whether this stays a sourcing-and-timing argument over gas allocation or escalates into a fiscal or contract renegotiation, since the latter path is the one that has historically affected operator economics and capex sequencing in comparable host-country standoffs. For the equity, single-project gas allocation in one jurisdiction has rarely been a standalone driver for an integrated major of this scale; the read-through sits more with Guyana's LNG ambitions and regional gas supply expectations than with Exxon's consolidated cash flow.

War-related disruptions in the Middle East scrambled energy markets, and Exxon still posted adjusted earnings of $14.7 billion, up from $8.8 billion in the first quarter. The business is easy to picture. Exxon pumps oil and gas worldwide, refines crude into gasoline and diesel at the pump, and turns other streams into chemicals and lubricants. When oil and fuel prices climb, profits usually follow. That's also the catch. Investors are paying more than usual for Exxon's earnings just as those earnings are expected to shrink. Whether that premium holds up depends on how much of Exxon's strength comes from the oil cycle, and how much comes from the company itself, a strategic expansion that includes lithium production and also positions it among the 10 Best Battery Stocks to Buy According to Billionaires. Exxon's edge starts with its integrated setup, running everything from wells to refineries to chemical plants. CEO Darren Woods credited that global portfolio with letting the company reroute products as markets shifted. The numbers back him up: Energy Products earned $5.465 billion on a GAAP basis, swinging from a $1.262 billion loss in the first quarter. Cost discipline is the quieter advantage. Exxon has banked $16.3 billion in cumulative structural cost savings since 2019. Cost control has become a key battleground among the world's integrated oil majors, a dynamic central to evaluating the 10 Best Oil and Gas Stocks to Buy for the Next Decade. Exxon says its savings exceed those of all its international peers combined, providing the kind of structural efficiency that sticks around when prices don't The growth pipeline points the same way. Permian production hit a record of more than 1.8 million oil-equivalent barrels per day, and Exxon plans 9% compound annual growth there through 2030. In Guyana, the fifth floating production vessel has set sail, with startup planned for the fourth quarter of 2026 and 250,000 barrels per day of added capacity. Cash backs it up. Free cash flow hit $17.2 billion in the quarter, and Exxon returned $9.4 billion to shareholders: $4.3 billion in dividends and $5.1 billion in buybacks. With a quarterly dividend of $1.03 per share, Exxon remains one of energy's most reliable dividend payers. Not everything was clean. Exxon booked $2.6 billion in identified charges, which is why GAAP earnings of $14.5 billion trailed the adjusted figure. It also estimated a $2.5 billion favorable boost from timing effects (accounting gains tied to price swings that tend to reverse). The strongest objection is that Exxon's blowout quarter rode a temporary wave. Oil markets remain jumpy, and in recent days traders have been weighing rising Middle East exports against renewed Gulf tensions, according to CNBC. If supply normalizes, prices could cool, and so could the windfalls that powered the quarter. Consensus forecasts echo that worry, with EPS expected to fall 8.36% in 2028. Exxon's cost cuts and Permian growth can cushion the blow, but they can't fully offset a lower price on every barrel sold. Exxon trades at 13.51 times forward earnings, as of October 9, above both its 5-year average of 12.91 and the sector's 12.30. Put simply, investors are paying more for each dollar of Exxon's expected profit than they usually do, and more than they pay for the typical energy stock. A premium normally rewards faster growth, and Exxon's outlook points the other way. So the multiple is pricing in something beyond near-term earnings: trust in the leaner cost base, the Permian and Guyana expansions, and the cash returns that come with them. Even as capital targets high-upside plays among the 10 Most Promising Energy Stocks to Buy Now, investors are willing to pay up for Exxon's defensive balance sheet and execution. There's little cushion in the multiple. If earnings drop as forecast and the valuation drifts back toward its historical norm, shareholders would feel both hits at once. Hedge funds appear to be leaning in anyway, with 89 holding the stock in the most recent quarter, up from 79 in the prior one. Short interest sits at just 1.08% of the float, a sign of relatively limited bearish positioning. Exxon looks like a stronger business than it was a few years ago, with lower costs, growing low-cost barrels, and hefty cash returns. But at 13.51 times forward earnings, the stock already prices in much of that progress, even as profits are expected to shrink. The setup suits patient, income-minded investors who value the dividend and buybacks over near-term upside. If you're counting on oil staying elevated, the math is less forgiving. A lasting slide in oil prices would change the picture, while a smooth Guyana startup and continued Permian growth would strengthen it. Broadcom Inc.’s AI chip business is showing little sign of slowing down, with the semiconductor giant expecting revenue from its AI chips to double in each of the next two years as demand from customers including Anthropic and OpenAI accelerates. The Palo Alto, California-based company expects AI semiconductor revenue to reach about $115 billion in fiscal 2027, up from roughly $58 billion expected in 2026, CEO Hock Tan said on the company’s third-quarter earnings call. The company sees another doubling to $230 billion in fiscal 2028, underscoring the strength of its custom AI accelerator and networking chip business. “In 2027, we have secured the supply to again double AI revenue to approximately $115 billion. Our demand actually exceeds this outlook, and we will work to improve supply,” Tan said. “In 2028… we have line of sight for fiscal 2028 AI semiconductor revenue growth to again double to $230 billion. Here again, we have secured the supply to meet this outlook.” Despite the strong outlook, Broadcom’s fourth-quarter revenue forecast, which implies 93% growth, came in below Wall Street’s expectations, sending AVGO shares 1.3% lower in overnight trading late Wednesday. The comments highlight how Broadcom has emerged as one of the biggest beneficiaries of the AI infrastructure boom beyond Nvidia. Its custom accelerators, or XPUs, are increasingly being adopted by major AI companies looking to build their own chips. AI chip sales more than tripled to $16.7 billion in the third quarter, lifting Broadcom's total revenue 86% to $29.59 billion, beating estimates of $29.36 billion. Adjusted profit came in at $3.32 ​per share, compared with estimates of $3.24. Anthropic is expected to become Broadcom’s largest XPU customer next year, with the AI startup planning to deploy another 5 gigawatts of Broadcom-designed TPU v8i chips in 2027 and an additional 10 gigawatts in 2028. OpenAI is also expected to become a major customer, with Broadcom seeing a path for the ChatGPT maker to deploy more than 5 gigawatts of its next-generation Jalapeno XPU in 2028. “These two guys, Anthropic and OpenAI, I mean, these are… it’s like you have two geniuses in the middle of outer Mongolia. They need to go to college to fulfill their potential,” Tan said, suggesting that while both companies have enormous potential, they need access to Broadcom’s chips and infrastructure (“college”) to fully realize it. “We do what we can to help them, and part of it is creating sources of financing to help these companies with the leading-edge frontier models in the world be able to play in the same playing field and be able to offer these great technology products to the world,” he added. Broadcom has secured supplies for wafers, substrates and memory needed to meet its 2027 and 2028 AI revenue targets. The company also plans to begin deploying its Singapore substrate facility in fiscal 2027 to ease a key supply bottleneck. Moor Insights & Strategy CEO and analyst Patrick Moorhead said Broadcom delivered a “strong, but not flawless” third quarter, arguing that the key takeaway was its AI execution rather than the modest revenue beat. He pointed to Broadcom’s $16.7 billion in Q3 AI revenue and $21.7 billion Q4 outlook as evidence that the company is successfully converting its AI backlog into sales. Moorhead also highlighted Broadcom’s broader AI infrastructure advantage, spanning custom XPU co-design, Ethernet switching, SerDes, optics, packaging and foundry access, but cautioned that the results “do not prove broad NVIDIA displacement.” “The wrinkle is software, and the release does not resolve customer concentration, Google multisourcing, bookings conversion, AI networking mix, first-generation XPU yields or the fiscal 2027 AI bridge,” he said. Future Fund Managing Director Gary Black noted the improvement in AVGO stock after-hours “as investors responded favorably to the company’s AI rev growth guidance”. “As the AI Rev strength becomes clearer to investors, I expect the stock to recover somewhat,” he said. AVGO was the top trending ticker on Stocktwits at the time of writing, with the retail sentiment for the stock turning ‘extremely bullish’ from ‘bullish’ the previous day. “$AVGO Broadcom just posted the most massive financial results in company history — bears can say whatever they want — the share price will go higher regardless,” a trader said. Another wrote: “$AVGO it takes time for the earnings results and outlook to filter into the market; this forward outlook is insane… The stock is too cheap, just like Nvidia.  It’s going higher.” AVGO stock declined in the two sessions leading up to the Q3 report and is up a mere 6.5% year to date. In comparison, the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) has gained over 65% over the same period. For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. Shares of Rocket Lab (RKLB) snapped a three-session losing streak on Wednesday after the space company completed its 94th Electron mission, with investors appearing to look past a regulatory filing disclosing an $8.77 million share sale by its CFO. RKLB stock rose 1% on Wednesday to finish the session at $63.10. However, the shares remain on track for their fourth consecutive weekly decline. Rocket Lab launched the “Owl Around The World” mission from its Mahia launch complex in New Zealand after high winds forced the company to postpone the flight twice. The Electron rocket successfully deployed Synspective’s latest StriX satellite into a 575-kilometer low-Earth orbit. The satellite uses synthetic aperture radar to capture images of the Earth’s surface regardless of cloud cover, weather conditions or daylight. Rocket Lab also developed a payload fairing specifically tailored to the dimensions of the StriX satellite. The company said Electron remains the world’s most frequently launched small orbital rocket. The mission marked Rocket Lab’s 15th launch of 2026 and 11th successful mission for Synspective, extending its perfect launch record for the Japanese satellite operator. The two companies began working together in 2020 as Synspective sought to build out its constellation of radar-imaging satellites. Another 16 dedicated Electron missions for Synspective remain booked through 2030, giving Rocket Lab a pipeline of repeat business from Synspective. The order book was expanded in June when Synspective signed on for 17 additional Electron launches. Wednesday’s flight was the first mission completed under the expanded commitment. Rocket Lab’s previous Electron flight, its 93rd overall, deployed another Earth-observation satellite for Japanese customer iQPS in August. Nine more dedicated launches for iQPS are booked through 2030. Spice acquired the shares on Wednesday through the exercise of stock options. The proposed transaction was arranged under a Rule 10b5-1 trading plan adopted on June 3. Spice also sold 56,303 Rocket Lab shares across three transactions in August, generating combined gross proceeds of about $4.45 million, the filing showed. title: Why Are BATL, TPET, XOM, CVX, USO, UCO Stocks Rising Overnight? - Stocktwits
content: Shares of multiple oil companies and oil exchange-traded funds climbed overnight late Sunday after Brent crude prices rose above $90 a barrel amid escalating tensions between the U.S. and Iran. Mohamed El-Erian, Chief Economic Advisor at Allianz, noted on X late Sunday, “Responding to this weekend's US-Iran escalation, Brent crude is currently above $90 a barrel in Asian trading.” WTI crude futures expiring in August also rose more than 2% to $84.33 per barrel. As a result, oil companies Battalion Oil Corp. (BATL) and Trio Petroleum Corp. (TPET) rose more than 7% and by over 8% in the overnight session. Oil majors Exxon Mobil Corp. (XOM) and Chevron Corp. (CVX) also rose about 1% each. Meanwhile, the United States Oil Fund (USO), which tracks the daily price movements of West Texas Intermediate (WTI), climbed more than 2% at the time of writing, while ProShares Ultra Bloomberg Crude Oil (UCO) rallied more than 3%. The Light, Sweet Crude Oil Futures (CL_F) were also 2% higher. Oil prices soared back up as tensions between the U.S. and Iran escalated over the weekend after the American military launched a ninth consecutive night of attacks on the Middle Eastern country. “CENTCOM began conducting a new wave of strikes against Iran at 7 p.m. ET today for the ninth consecutive night. The strikes will continue degrading Iranian military capabilities used to attack commercial vessels and civilian mariners transiting the Strait of Hormuz,” the U.S. Central Command said in a post on X. Over the weekend, CENTCOM confirmed that a third U.S. service member had died following recent fighting in the Middle East. The military had initially reported two fatalities and one service member missing after an Iranian attack in Jordan on July 17 before later confirming the third death. Meanwhile, Iran Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi condemned the U.S. strike on the under-construction Darquoin power plant, calling it a dangerous attack on Iran's civilian infrastructure. In a post on X, he said the strike made Washington fully responsible for the resulting instability and warned that Iran would take appropriate measures to safeguard its national security and interests. "The longer the Strait remains closed and the war escalates the greater ​the risk that oil prices will have to rise to around $150/barrel to bring demand down to match the hit to supply," Shane Oliver, Head of Investment Strategy and Chief Economist, at AMP reportedly told Reuters, adding that "This is not our base case but it's a high risk again." Meanwhile, Garfield Reynolds, MLIV Asia team leader at Bloomberg, reportedly said the widening spread between Brent crude and WTI reflects growing concerns that an escalation in the U.S.-Iran conflict could disrupt global energy supplies, though the gap remains narrow enough that equity markets have largely shrugged off the risk compared with the early stages of the war. Analyst Patrick De Haan said on X that rising oil prices would likely send gas prices higher in the U.S. in the coming week. “Brent crude oil up ~3% reaching $90/bbl, while WTI crude up ~2% to nearly $85/bbl. RBOB up 5c/gal, national average gas price will hit $4/gal either tomorrow or Tuesday, likely to see increases ahead for most states!” he said. After a period in which the alliance had been gradually restoring barrels it had earlier withheld, the choice to stand pat signaled a more measured stance toward balancing global demand against available supply. For the wider oil complex, that kind of restraint tends to put a floor under prices during soft stretches, and it helped crude settle into a steadier band rather than drifting lower. News of the supply pause circulated quickly as trading opened, and energy names featured prominently in coverage of the day's corporate and commodity headlines. Market participants spent the session weighing what a steadier crude band might mean for the largest producers, and the integrated structure of this company placed it near the center of that conversation. What sets this company apart within the sector is the breadth of its operations, which span the full chain from the wellhead to the finished product. On the upstream side, the group explores for and produces crude and natural gas across a wide geographic footprint. The production arm of the company reaches across continents, from long-established basins to newer developments that have reshaped its output in recent years. A prominent strand of that effort has been its expanding presence in offshore developments and in low-cost onshore acreage, where the group has sought to concentrate its drilling where barrels can be produced efficiently. The refining operation sits at the heart of the company's downstream presence, turning crude into gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, and a range of other products that move through the global economy. Refining margins hinge on the gap between the cost of crude feedstock and the price of finished fuels, a spread that can widen when raw-material costs ease. Beyond fuels, the company operates a substantial chemicals business that converts hydrocarbons into plastics, performance materials, and specialty products used across packaging, construction, automotive, and consumer goods. The chemicals arm adds another layer of diversification, since its fortunes are tied to industrial demand and feedstock costs rather than to the price of crude alone. A range-bound crude market places particular emphasis on how capital is managed. Rather than ramping spending aggressively in response to every price move, the largest integrated majors have leaned toward steadiness, channeling capital toward their most advantaged projects while keeping a firm grip on costs. The supply pause arrives during a watchful stretch for energy broadly. Alongside crude, natural gas has grown into an increasingly important part of the energy conversation, and the company maintains a meaningful position across gas production and the chilled, liquefied form that moves across oceans. Demand for cleaner-burning fuel has supported interest in gas as economies weigh how to balance reliability against lower emissions, and the largest majors have been expanding their presence in this corner of the market. title: Exxon Mobil Holdings (XOM) Q1 2026 Earnings Call Transcript - Fortune
content:
Jim ChapmanGood morning, everyone. Welcome to ExxonMobil's earnings call. Today's call is being recorded. We appreciate you joining us. I'm Jim Chapman and I'm joined by Darren Woods, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, and Neil Hansen, Senior Vice President and Chief Financial Officer. This quarter's presentation and prerecorded remarks are available on the investors section of our website. They're meant to accompany this quarter's earnings release, which is posted in the same location. During today's presentation, we'll make forward-looking remarks, including comments on our long-term plans, which are subject to risks and uncertainties. Please read our cautionary statement on slide two. You can find more information on the risks and uncertainties that apply to any forward-looking statements in our SEC filings on our website. We also provide supplemental information at the end of our earnings slides, which are also posted on our website. Now I'll turn it over to Darren for opening remarks. Darren WoodsGood morning, and thank you for joining us. Let me begin by recognizing the impact of the conflict in the Middle East on our colleagues and partners in the region. We've been in close contact with our regional partners, as well as with companies and countries we have worked with for many years. We are proud to stand beside them during these very difficult times. While the financial impact in the region is real, what is even more real is the daily threat our colleagues and partners have been living under. We remain committed to supporting them as we work to restore operations and repair assets with a clear focus on safety and disciplined risk management. The Middle East is and will continue to be an advantaged and meaningful component of our global portfolio. The disruption to the broader economy we are seeing underscores the critical role our company plays in providing the affordable, reliable energy and products the world depends on. What we produce remains essential to development and progress, sustaining and improving living standards around the world. In this environment, scale, integration, and execution excellence matters. Those advantages, combined with the deep experience and capability of our employees, give us the ability to respond quickly and manage effectively through disruptions. Our competitive advantages are on display in this quarter's results. We delivered strong operational performance in a challenging environment, maintained rigorous safety and reliability standards, and continued advancing key priorities across the portfolio, supporting long-term value creation for our shareholders. We saw those advantages in our response to supply disruptions, leveraging our global portfolio to support customers. We delivered on our plans to increase Permian production year-over-year, achieved record levels of production in Guyana, achieved first LNG at Golden Pass, optimized logistics and crude product flows, and safely maximized refinery throughput where possible. In fact, in March, refinery throughput increased by approximately 200,000bbl a day versus February, or the equivalent of a mid-sized refinery. As we brought back refineries from turnaround and deferred maintenance activities where we could without impacting safety or long-term reliability. Our global supply chain organization rapidly executed alternate routings from the U.S. Gulf Coast to Asia to sustain critical supplies for our customers. Despite the unprecedented impacts in the global energy system, we maintained deliveries to our customers globally through coordinated planning and real-time vessel visibility. Financially, excluding identified items and estimated timing effects, our first quarter earnings per share were up versus the fourth quarter of 2025, reflecting the strength and resiliency of the underlying business. Stronger portfolio mix, structural cost reductions, and execution excellence continue to drive improving performance. Those same factors leave us better positioned to manage uncertainty versus several years ago. The strength of that advantage portfolio is clear in the work we're doing today. We are expanding our LNG footprint. Our newest facility, Golden Pass LNG, a joint venture with QatarEnergy, is increasing U.S. export capacity at an important moment for global supply. Train 1 of the facility achieved first LNG in March and will deliver an increase of about 5% relative to 2025 U.S. exports. By the time the third train is online, we will increase the country's current LNG exports by roughly 15%. At the same time, we continue to progress toward final investment decisions on LNG projects in Papua New Guinea and Mozambique, both expected later this year. Elsewhere in the upstream, Guyana continues to set the standard for execution, development pace, and value creation. We delivered record production, continued strong reliability, and have Uaru, Whiptail, and Hammerhead projects under construction, with Uaru expecting first oil late this year. Consistent with our broader approach to support long-term economic development in countries where we operate, we've committed a $100 million investment over 10 years to support national STEM education in Guyana, strengthening our bond with the people of Guyana and establishing a foundation for long-term prosperity. In the Permian, we continue to show how scale and proprietary technologies improve efficiency, recovery, and long-term value creation. We remain on track to grow full-year Permian production to 1.8 million oil equivalent barrels in 2026, with that growth grounded in value, not volume. We're also progressing our Permian net zero ambition with continuous methane monitoring implemented across all key assets in New Mexico. In product solutions, performance remains strong, driven by higher value products and technology-led differentiation. The Beaumont Refinery expansion, completed in 2023, fully recovered its initial investment ahead of expectation and is contributing to stronger margins and cash flow. This underscores how disciplined investments grounded in long-term market fundamentals rigorously executed generate durable returns independent of price cycles. In parallel, we continue to progress our journey to build a reliable domestic supply of advanced synthetic graphite. We recently held a ribbon-cutting ceremony at the pilot production plant in Kentucky, which represents a critical milestone between lab-scale development and full commercial deployment. In low-carbon solutions, we began transporting and storing captured CO2 from the New Generation Gas Gathering project, our second startup in less than a year. Through this year and next, we plan to start facilities with the capacity to capture an additional 4 million tons per year of CO2. Importantly, with our advantages, these projects deliver attractive returns that compete with the investments in our base business. Technology as a core competitive advantage remains central to our strategy, is one of the ways we improve structural competitiveness, strengthen returns, and create new earnings opportunity. In Guyana, we achieved the first deep water fully autonomous well section using rig automation and automated downhole steering tools, improving both safety and efficiency. Additionally, we're on track to leverage our Proxxima technology in subsea applications with Hammerhead and future FPSOs, further demonstrating the material's performance in demanding offshore environments. Across the company, we're making further progress to simplify how we run the business through effective application of technology. Our enterprise-wide process and data platform transformation, the largest ever undertaken in the industry, reached an important milestone with the successful launch of a new modern workforce enablement system. This significantly simplifies the work processes that underpin our talent management approach and streamlines our payroll processes in more than 50 countries. It provides a single, consistent data foundation on which future system deployments will be built. We deliver this with no business disruption, demonstrating the strength of our centralized core capabilities, fully leveraging our scale advantage. This is the first step of many to make our processes more efficient and effective, ultimately enhancing the experience of our global workforce.
